C3. Trade-offs between classical ML and deep learning¶

Dimension HOG + RBF-SVM (classical) Custom CNN (deep learning)
Test accuracy / macro F1 0.644 / 0.643 0.877 / 0.875 (+23 points)
Features Hand-engineered by a human (edges + colour); limited to what the designer anticipated Learned automatically from raw pixels, from edges up to object parts
Hardest classes (F1) cat (0.45), dog (0.52), bird (0.53) cat (0.76), dog (0.81), bird (0.84): the same classes, but far less severe. The biggest CNN gains are exactly on these animal classes (+0.29 to +0.31 F1)
Overfitting Severe: 99.7% train vs 63% validation accuracy; 38,286 of 45,000 training images (85%) became support vectors, i.e. the model largely memorises the data Well controlled: best validation accuracy (88.1%) is almost identical to test accuracy (87.7%) thanks to dropout, batch normalisation, augmentation and early stopping. (Its training accuracy, 85.9%, appears lower only because it is measured on augmented images with dropout active.)
Compute ~2.5 min on a laptop CPU, no GPU needed ~15 min on a T4 GPU; would take hours on a CPU
Model size / inference Stores 38k support vectors (~37 MB); ~5 ms per image, and inference cost grows with training-set size 3.4M parameters (~13 MB of weights); fast batched inference, cost independent of training-set size
Data needs & scaling Kernel SVM training scales roughly quadratically with the number of samples, so it does not scale to much larger datasets Improves with more data; mini-batch training scales to millions of images
Interpretability Pipeline steps are transparent, but after PCA + RBF kernel individual decisions are hard to explain A black box, but Grad-CAM shows which pixels drove each decision (Part D)
Robustness (Part E) Almost unaffected by darkening; weak under over-exposure Much more accurate overall, but loses 26 points on very dark images
Validation used Stratified 5-fold CV (cheap enough to repeat 5 times) Single hold-out split + early stopping (5-fold CV would cost ~5× the GPU time)

Why did transfer learning (EfficientNetB0) underperform? Despite being pre-trained on ImageNet, it reached only 56.7%. Likely causes: the 32×32 images are upscaled to 96×96, so the pre-trained filters see blurry, unnatural inputs; only 10 + 10 epochs of training were used; and its training accuracy (53.9%) was lower than its validation accuracy (57.0%), indicating underfitting rather than overfitting. With larger input resolution and longer fine-tuning it would be expected to surpass the custom CNN.

Conclusion: for this task the custom CNN is clearly superior in predictive performance (+23 accuracy points, better on every class) and generalisation. The classical SVM remains useful as a cheap, CPU-only baseline that quantifies how much value representation learning adds.

Part D: Explainability (XAI)¶

Accuracy tells us how often a model is right, not why. Explainability methods let us check whether a model relies on the object itself or on shortcuts (e.g. background colour), which matters for trust, debugging and fairness. We use three complementary techniques:

Technique Model Scope What it answers
Grouped permutation importance Classical SVM Global Which image regions and which feature types (shape vs colour) does the model depend on overall?
LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations) Classical SVM (model-agnostic, so it also works for the CNN) Local (one image) Which superpixels pushed the model towards or away from its prediction for this image?
Grad-CAM CNN Local (one image) Which pixels in the last convolutional layer's feature maps drove the CNN's decision?

Tools: the lime library (reference implementation by the method's authors) and scikit-learn utilities; Grad-CAM is implemented directly in TensorFlow using GradientTape.

In [ ]:
# ====================================================
# D1. SETUP: SVM MODEL AND PREDICTION HELPERS
# ====================================================
import os, json, joblib
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from joblib import Parallel, delayed

if 'svm_model' not in globals():
    svm_model = joblib.load('artifacts/svm_pipeline.joblib')
svm_test_pred = np.load('artifacts/svm_test_pred.npy')

def svm_scores(images):
    """Softmax-normalised SVM decision scores. The RBF-SVM has no native probabilities,
    so these pseudo-probabilities are used as the score function for LIME."""
    feats = np.array([extract_features(im) for im in images])
    s = svm_model.decision_function(feats)
    e = np.exp(s - s.max(axis=1, keepdims=True))
    return e / e.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)

print(f"SVM test accuracy (from Part B): {(svm_test_pred == lbl_test).mean():.4f}")

SVM test accuracy (from Part B): 0.6436

D2. Global explanation: grouped permutation importance (SVM)¶

For each group of features we randomly shuffle its values across images and measure how much test accuracy drops. A large drop means the model depends heavily on that group.

  • Spatial groups: the HOG descriptor is made of a 7Ã—7 grid of overlapping blocks, each covering an 8Ã—8-pixel patch. Shuffling one block shows how important that region of the image is.
  • Feature-type groups: all HOG features (shape/edges) vs all colour-histogram features (hue, saturation, brightness).
In [4]:
# ====================================================
# D2. GROUPED PERMUTATION IMPORTANCE ON 2,000 TEST IMAGES
# ====================================================
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
perm_idx = rng.choice(len(X_test_feat), 2000, replace=False)
X_perm_base, y_perm_base = X_test_feat[perm_idx], lbl_test[perm_idx]

N_BLOCKS, BLOCK_LEN = 7, 2 * 2 * 9          # 7x7 HOG blocks, each = 2x2 cells x 9 orientations
N_HOG = N_BLOCKS * N_BLOCKS * BLOCK_LEN      # 1,764 HOG features, followed by 48 colour features

def block_columns(r, c):
    start = (r * N_BLOCKS + c) * BLOCK_LEN
    return np.arange(start, start + BLOCK_LEN)

# Group the 7x7 blocks into a 3x3 grid of regions: block rows/cols 0-1 | 2-4 | 5-6
region_spans = [range(0, 2), range(2, 5), range(5, 7)]
feature_groups = {f'region_{i}_{j}': np.concatenate([block_columns(r, c) for r in rows for c in cols])
                  for i, rows in enumerate(region_spans) for j, cols in enumerate(region_spans)}
feature_groups.update({
    'All shape features (HOG)': np.arange(N_HOG),
    'All colour features': np.arange(N_HOG, N_HOG + 48),
    'Hue histogram': np.arange(N_HOG, N_HOG + 16),
    'Saturation histogram': np.arange(N_HOG + 16, N_HOG + 32),
    'Brightness (value) histogram': np.arange(N_HOG + 32, N_HOG + 48),
})

base_acc = (svm_model.predict(X_perm_base) == y_perm_base).mean()

N_REPEATS = 3

def accuracy_drop(cols, seed):
    X_shuffled = X_perm_base.copy()
    X_shuffled[:, cols] = X_perm_base[np.random.default_rng(seed).permutation(len(X_perm_base))][:, cols]
    return base_acc - (svm_model.predict(X_shuffled) == y_perm_base).mean()

jobs = [(name, rep) for name in feature_groups for rep in range(N_REPEATS)]
results = Parallel(n_jobs=-1)(delayed(accuracy_drop)(feature_groups[name], 1000 * rep + k)
                              for k, (name, rep) in enumerate(jobs))
drops = pd.DataFrame(jobs, columns=['group', 'rep']).assign(drop=results).groupby('group', sort=False)['drop'].mean().to_dict()
print(f"Baseline accuracy on the 2,000-image subset: {base_acc:.4f}")

spatial = np.array([[drops[f'region_{i}_{j}'] for j in range(3)] for i in range(3)])
type_groups = ['All shape features (HOG)', 'All colour features', 'Hue histogram',
               'Saturation histogram', 'Brightness (value) histogram']

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(15, 5.5), gridspec_kw={'width_ratios': [1, 1.4]})
sns.heatmap(spatial * 100, annot=True, fmt='.1f', cmap='Reds', square=True, ax=axes[0],
            cbar_kws={'label': 'Accuracy drop (percentage points)'})
axes[0].set_title('Where does the SVM look?\nAccuracy drop when each image region is shuffled')
axes[0].set_xticklabels(['left', 'centre', 'right']); axes[0].set_yticklabels(['top', 'middle', 'bottom'], rotation=0)
vals = [drops[g] * 100 for g in type_groups]
bars = axes[1].barh(type_groups[::-1], vals[::-1],
                    color=['#56B4E9', '#56B4E9', '#56B4E9', '#E69F00', '#0072B2'])
axes[1].bar_label(bars, fmt='%.1f pts', padding=3)
axes[1].set_xlabel('Accuracy drop (percentage points)')
axes[1].set_title('Shape vs colour: which feature types matter?')
axes[1].set_xlim(0, max(vals) * 1.2)
plt.suptitle('SVM global explanation: grouped permutation importance', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig('figures/xai_svm_permutation_importance.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
plt.show()

print(f"Accuracy drop when shuffling the centre region: {spatial[1, 1] * 100:.1f} pts | "
      f"mean over the 8 outer regions: {(spatial.sum() - spatial[1, 1]) / 8 * 100:.1f} pts")
for g in type_groups:
    print(f"{g:32s}: {drops[g] * 100:5.1f} pts")

D3. Local explanations: LIME (SVM)¶

LIME splits an image into ~30 superpixels (SLIC segmentation), creates 1,000 perturbed copies with random superpixels greyed out (replaced by their mean colour), records how the model's score changes, and fits a simple linear model to estimate each superpixel's contribution. Blue regions support the predicted class; red regions push against it.

The same six test images (three correct predictions, three typical errors of the SVM) are reused for Grad-CAM so the two models can be compared side by side.

In [ ]:
# ====================================================
# D3. LIME EXPLANATIONS FOR SIX TEST IMAGES
# ====================================================
from lime import lime_image
from lime.wrappers.scikit_image import SegmentationAlgorithm

# Pick deterministic examples: (true class, SVM-predicted class)
example_pairs = [(0, 0), (1, 1), (7, 7),   # correct: airplane, automobile, horse
                 (3, 5), (5, 3), (2, 0)]   # errors: cat->dog, dog->cat, bird->airplane
xai_indices = [int(np.where((lbl_test == t) & (svm_test_pred == p))[0][0]) for t, p in example_pairs]
with open('artifacts/xai_indices.json', 'w') as f:
    json.dump(xai_indices, f)

explainer = lime_image.LimeImageExplainer(random_state=42)
segmenter = SegmentationAlgorithm('slic', n_segments=30, compactness=10, start_label=0)

lime_maps = {}
for idx in xai_indices:
    exp = explainer.explain_instance(img_test[idx], svm_scores, top_labels=1, num_samples=1000,
                                     segmentation_fn=segmenter, batch_size=250, random_seed=42)
    label = exp.top_labels[0]
    weights = dict(exp.local_exp[label])
    lime_maps[idx] = (label, np.vectorize(lambda s: weights.get(s, 0.0))(exp.segments))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, len(xai_indices), figsize=(3 * len(xai_indices), 6.6))
for col, idx in enumerate(xai_indices):
    label, heat = lime_maps[idx]
    lim = np.abs(heat).max() or 1
    correct = lbl_test[idx] == svm_test_pred[idx]
    axes[0, col].imshow(img_test[idx])
    axes[0, col].set_title(f"True: {class_names[lbl_test[idx]]}\nSVM: {class_names[svm_test_pred[idx]]}",
                           color='green' if correct else 'red', fontsize=11)
    axes[1, col].imshow(img_test[idx])
    axes[1, col].imshow(heat, cmap='RdBu', vmin=-lim, vmax=lim, alpha=0.6)
    axes[1, col].set_title('LIME (blue = supports)', fontsize=10)
    for r in range(2):
        axes[r, col].axis('off')
plt.suptitle('SVM local explanations with LIME', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig('figures/xai_svm_lime.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
plt.show()

# How much of the positive evidence lies on the image border (background) vs the centre (usually the object)?
border_mask = np.ones((32, 32), bool); border_mask[6:26, 6:26] = False
for idx in xai_indices:
    pos = np.clip(lime_maps[idx][1], 0, None)
    share = pos[border_mask].sum() / pos.sum() if pos.sum() > 0 else float('nan')
    print(f"Image {idx:5d} ({class_names[lbl_test[idx]]:>10s} -> {class_names[svm_test_pred[idx]]:<10s}): "
          f"{share:.0%} of supporting evidence is in the outer border (border = {border_mask.mean():.0%} of pixels)")

Image     3 (  airplane -> airplane  ): 45% of supporting evidence is in the outer border (border = 61% of pixels)
Image     6 (automobile -> automobile): 50% of supporting evidence is in the outer border (border = 61% of pixels)
Image    13 (     horse -> horse     ): 42% of supporting evidence is in the outer border (border = 61% of pixels)
Image    61 (       cat -> dog       ): 49% of supporting evidence is in the outer border (border = 61% of pixels)
Image   361 (       dog -> cat       ): 70% of supporting evidence is in the outer border (border = 61% of pixels)
Image    70 (      bird -> airplane  ): 68% of supporting evidence is in the outer border (border = 61% of pixels)

D4. What the explanations reveal about the SVM¶

1. The SVM is almost purely a shape model. Shuffling all HOG features drops accuracy by 54.7 points (from 65% to ~10%, i.e. random guessing), while shuffling all colour features costs only 1.8 points. The colour histograms we engineered add almost nothing. The model recognises objects from edge orientations alone.

2. It looks mainly at the centre of the image. The centre region is by far the most important (13.1-point drop) compared with an average of 4.3 points for the eight outer regions, and the middle row/centre column matter more than the corners. This matches how CIFAR-10 was built (objects are roughly centred), but it also means the model would struggle with off-centre objects in real use.

3. Errors are often driven by the background (LIME). For the three correct predictions, only 42-50% of the supporting evidence lies in the outer border, even though the border covers 61% of the pixels, so evidence is concentrated on the object. For two of the three errors the pattern reverses: 70% (dog → cat) and 68% (bird → airplane) of the supporting evidence comes from the background. The bird is classified as an airplane largely because of the smooth, pale, sky-like background around it: the model has learned a spurious correlation between plain backgrounds and airplanes.

Limitations: LIME explains six individual images only, so these local findings are illustrative rather than statistical, and LIME's output depends on the superpixel segmentation and random sampling. Permutation importance is computed on 2,000 test images and averaged over 3 repeats, so it is the more reliable global finding.

Comparison with the CNN: the next section explains the CNN on the same six images, with both LIME (same method as above, for a like-for-like comparison) and Grad-CAM.

D5. Explaining the CNN: Grad-CAM and LIME¶

Grad-CAM (Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping) takes the feature maps of the CNN's last convolutional layer (conv3_2, an 8×8 grid of 256 channels), weights each channel by how strongly the predicted class score depends on it (its average gradient), and sums them into a heatmap. Bright regions are those that most increased the score of the predicted class. Unlike LIME, it uses the network's internal gradients, so it is fast and exact, but it only works for CNNs.

To compare the two models like for like, LIME is also run on the CNN with the same settings as for the SVM. Finally, Grad-CAM is averaged over 1,000 test images to see where the CNN looks in general.

In [ ]:
# ====================================================
# D5. GRAD-CAM AND LIME FOR THE CNN ON THE SAME SIX IMAGES
# ====================================================
import tensorflow as tf

if 'cnn_model' not in globals() or cnn_model is None:
    cnn_model = load_saved_cnn()
assert cnn_model is not None, "The trained CNN is required: run Part A or place custom_cnn_model.keras in this folder."

def cnn_scores(images):
    """CNN class probabilities for uint8 images (same preprocessing as in training: scale to 0-1)."""
    return cnn_model.predict(np.asarray(images).astype('float32') / 255.0, verbose=0, batch_size=256)

def grad_cam(image, layer_name='conv3_2', class_idx=None):
    """Grad-CAM heatmap (32x32, values 0-1) for one uint8 image."""
    x = tf.convert_to_tensor(image[None].astype('float32') / 255.0)
    with tf.GradientTape() as tape:
        h, feature_maps = x, None
        for layer in cnn_model.layers[:-1]:     # forward pass, keeping the target layer's output
            h = layer(h, training=False)
            if layer.name == layer_name:
                feature_maps = h
                tape.watch(feature_maps)
        output_layer = cnn_model.layers[-1]      # use pre-softmax logits (softmax saturates gradients)
        logits = tf.matmul(h, output_layer.kernel) + output_layer.bias
        if class_idx is None:
            class_idx = int(tf.argmax(logits[0]))
        class_score = logits[:, class_idx]
    grads = tape.gradient(class_score, feature_maps)             # d(score) / d(feature map)
    channel_weights = tf.reduce_mean(grads, axis=(0, 1, 2))      # one weight per channel
    cam = tf.nn.relu(tf.reduce_sum(feature_maps[0] * channel_weights, axis=-1))
    cam = cam / (tf.reduce_max(cam) + 1e-8)
    return tf.image.resize(cam[..., None], (32, 32), method='bilinear')[..., 0].numpy(), class_idx

cnn_pred_examples = np.argmax(cnn_scores(img_test[xai_indices]), axis=1)
cnn_lime_maps = {}
for idx in xai_indices:
    exp = explainer.explain_instance(img_test[idx], cnn_scores, top_labels=1, num_samples=1000,
                                     segmentation_fn=segmenter, batch_size=250, random_seed=42)
    weights = dict(exp.local_exp[exp.top_labels[0]])
    cnn_lime_maps[idx] = np.vectorize(lambda s: weights.get(s, 0.0))(exp.segments)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(4, len(xai_indices), figsize=(3 * len(xai_indices), 13))
row_titles = ['Image', 'SVM: LIME', 'CNN: LIME', 'CNN: Grad-CAM']
for col, idx in enumerate(xai_indices):
    svm_ok = svm_test_pred[idx] == lbl_test[idx]
    cnn_ok = cnn_pred_examples[col] == lbl_test[idx]
    axes[0, col].imshow(img_test[idx])
    axes[0, col].set_title(f"True: {class_names[lbl_test[idx]]}", fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')
    for row, (heat, model_name, pred, ok) in enumerate(
            [(lime_maps[idx][1], 'SVM', svm_test_pred[idx], svm_ok),
             (cnn_lime_maps[idx], 'CNN', cnn_pred_examples[col], cnn_ok)], start=1):
        lim = np.abs(heat).max() or 1
        axes[row, col].imshow(img_test[idx])
        axes[row, col].imshow(heat, cmap='RdBu', vmin=-lim, vmax=lim, alpha=0.6)
        axes[row, col].set_title(f"{model_name}: {class_names[pred]}", color='green' if ok else 'red', fontsize=10)
    cam, _ = grad_cam(img_test[idx])
    axes[3, col].imshow(img_test[idx])
    axes[3, col].imshow(cam, cmap='jet', alpha=0.45)
    axes[3, col].set_title(f"CNN: {class_names[cnn_pred_examples[col]]}", color='green' if cnn_ok else 'red', fontsize=10)
    for row in range(4):
        axes[row, col].set_xticks([]); axes[row, col].set_yticks([])
for row, title in enumerate(row_titles):
    axes[row, 0].set_ylabel(title, fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
plt.suptitle('Same images, two models: LIME (blue = supports prediction) and Grad-CAM (red = most important)',
             fontsize=13, fontweight='bold')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig('figures/xai_svm_vs_cnn.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
plt.show()

def border_share(heat):
    pos = np.clip(heat, 0, None)
    return pos[border_mask].sum() / pos.sum() if pos.sum() > 0 else np.nan

share_table = pd.DataFrame({
    'True class': [class_names[lbl_test[i]] for i in xai_indices],
    'SVM prediction': [class_names[svm_test_pred[i]] for i in xai_indices],
    'CNN prediction': [class_names[p] for p in cnn_pred_examples],
    'SVM LIME: evidence in border': [border_share(lime_maps[i][1]) for i in xai_indices],
    'CNN LIME: evidence in border': [border_share(cnn_lime_maps[i]) for i in xai_indices],
    'CNN Grad-CAM: evidence in border': [border_share(grad_cam(img_test[i])[0]) for i in xai_indices],
}, index=xai_indices)
print(f"Share of supporting evidence in the outer border (which covers {border_mask.mean():.0%} of the pixels):")
display(share_table.style.format({c: '{:.0%}' for c in share_table.columns if 'border' in c}))

cams = np.array([grad_cam(img_test[i])[0] for i in cam_idx])

D6. Comparing what the two models look at¶

Image SVM prediction CNN prediction SVM LIME evidence in border CNN LIME evidence in border CNN Grad-CAM evidence in border
airplane airplane ✓ airplane ✓ 45% 65% 37%
automobile automobile ✓ automobile ✓ 50% 36% 36%
horse horse ✓ horse ✓ 42% 33% 15%
cat dog ✗ dog ✗ 49% 42% 31%
dog cat ✗ dog ✓ 70% 25% 34%
bird airplane ✗ bird ✓ 68% 31% 23%

(The outer border covers 61% of the pixels, so values well below 61% mean the evidence is concentrated on the centre, where the object usually is.)

1. The CNN relies on the object, the SVM partly on the background. On the two images the SVM got wrong because of background evidence (dog, bird), the CNN puts only 25-34% of its evidence in the border and classifies both correctly. Grad-CAM highlights the dog's face and the bird's body, whereas the SVM was misled by the plain, sky-like background around the bird.

2. Averaged over 1,000 test images, the CNN looks at the centre. Only 38% of Grad-CAM evidence falls in the border region (61% of the pixels). For correct predictions this is 37%; for wrong predictions it rises to 47% and the heatmap becomes diffuse. When the CNN fails, it is often because it could not locate the object and spread its attention over the background, a useful diagnostic signal.

3. The two models fail in different ways. Both misclassify the cat as a dog, but for different reasons: the SVM's evidence is spread over the image, while Grad-CAM shows the CNN looking at the cat itself. Its error is a fine-grained confusion between two similar animals, not a background shortcut. The airplane is a case where the CNN's LIME evidence lies largely in the border (65%): the surrounding sky is genuinely informative for airplanes, which illustrates that "background" evidence is not always wrong but can become a shortcut.

4. The two explanation methods agree. LIME (model-agnostic, perturbation-based) and Grad-CAM (gradient-based, CNN-specific) highlight the same regions for the CNN, which increases confidence in the explanations.

Implication for deployment: explanations support the CNN as the more trustworthy model: its decisions are mostly based on the object itself. They also give a practical monitoring tool: a diffuse or border-heavy Grad-CAM map can flag predictions that deserve human review.

Part E: Bias and Diagnostic Analysis¶

CIFAR-10 contains no people, so there are no demographic attributes. The relevant risk for a vision system is that performance depends on image-capture conditions: a model that only works in good lighting will fail systematically for whoever (or wherever) produces darker, low-contrast or washed-out images, e.g. night-time cameras, cheaper sensors or poorly lit environments. We therefore define three subgroups on the test set, each split into equal-sized terciles:

Attribute Measured as Subgroups
Lighting mean luminance of the image Dark / Medium / Bright
Contrast standard deviation of luminance Low / Medium / High
Colourfulness mean HSV saturation Muted (near-greyscale) / Medium / Vivid

We then (1) compare accuracy, macro recall and macro F1 per subgroup with 95% confidence intervals, (2) test whether differences are statistically significant, (3) check whether subgroups differ in class composition (a confounder), and (4) run a controlled experiment that artificially darkens/brightens the same images.

The analysis covers every model available: the SVM always, and the CNN when custom_cnn_model.h5 (saved by Part A) is in the notebook folder or the model is in memory.

In [ ]:
# ====================================================
# E1. DEFINE SUBGROUPS FROM IMAGE PROPERTIES
# ====================================================
from skimage.color import rgb2hsv

luminance = (img_test.astype(np.float32) / 255) @ np.array([0.2125, 0.7154, 0.0721], dtype=np.float32)
brightness = luminance.mean(axis=(1, 2))
contrast = luminance.std(axis=(1, 2))
saturation = rgb2hsv(img_test)[..., 1].mean(axis=(1, 2))

subgroups = pd.DataFrame({
    'Lighting': pd.qcut(brightness, 3, labels=['Dark', 'Medium', 'Bright']),
    'Contrast': pd.qcut(contrast, 3, labels=['Low', 'Medium', 'High']),
    'Colourfulness': pd.qcut(saturation, 3, labels=['Muted', 'Medium', 'Vivid']),
    'label': lbl_test,
})
subgroups.to_csv('artifacts/test_subgroups.csv', index_label='test_index')

# Example images per lighting subgroup
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 8, figsize=(14, 5.6))
for r, grp in enumerate(['Dark', 'Medium', 'Bright']):
    for c, idx in enumerate(np.where(subgroups['Lighting'] == grp)[0][:8]):
        axes[r, c].imshow(img_test[idx]); axes[r, c].axis('off')
    axes[r, 0].set_title(grp, loc='left', fontsize=12, fontweight='bold')
plt.suptitle('Test images by lighting subgroup (mean luminance terciles)', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig('figures/bias_lighting_examples.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
plt.show()

# Class composition per lighting group (confounding check)
composition = pd.crosstab(subgroups['Lighting'], subgroups['label'].map(dict(enumerate(class_names))),
                          normalize='index') * 100
plt.figure(figsize=(12, 3.6))
sns.heatmap(composition, annot=True, fmt='.0f', cmap='Purples', cbar_kws={'label': '% of subgroup'})
plt.title('Class composition of each lighting subgroup (%): subgroups are NOT class-balanced')
plt.xlabel(''); plt.ylabel('')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig('figures/bias_lighting_class_composition.png', dpi=150, bbox_inches='tight')
plt.show()

# ====================================================
# E2. SUBGROUP PERFORMANCE FOR EVERY AVAILABLE MODEL
# ====================================================
from sklearn.metrics import f1_score, recall_score
from scipy.stats import chi2_contingency

def load_cnn_if_available(paths=('custom_cnn_model.keras', 'custom_cnn_model.h5')):
    """Use the CNN from Part A if it is in memory, otherwise load a saved copy if one exists."""
    if 'custom_model' in globals():
        return custom_model
    for path in paths:
        if os.path.exists(path):
            try:
                from tensorflow import keras
                return keras.models.load_model(path, compile=False)
            except ImportError:
                print("TensorFlow is not installed, so the CNN cannot be loaded.")
                return None
    print("No saved CNN found: running the bias analysis for the SVM only.")
    return None

cnn_for_analysis = load_cnn_if_available()

def cnn_predict_images(images):
    return np.argmax(cnn_for_analysis.predict(images.astype('float32') / 255.0, verbose=0, batch_size=256), axis=1)

def svm_predict_images(images):
    return svm_model.predict(extract_all(images))

predictors = {'HOG + RBF-SVM': svm_predict_images}
test_predictions = {'HOG + RBF-SVM': svm_test_pred}
if cnn_for_analysis is not None:
    predictors['Custom CNN'] = cnn_predict_images
    test_predictions['Custom CNN'] = cnn_predict_images(img_test)
model_colours = {'HOG + RBF-SVM': '#E69F00', 'Custom CNN': '#0072B2'}

def wilson_ci(k, n, z=1.96):
    p = k / n; denom = 1 + z ** 2 / n
    centre = (p + z ** 2 / (2 * n)) / denom
    half = z * np.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n + z ** 2 / (4 * n ** 2)) / denom
    return centre - half, centre + half

rows = []
for model_name, pred in test_predictions.items():
    for attr in ['Lighting', 'Contrast', 'Colourfulness']:
        for grp in subgroups[attr].cat.categories:
            m = (subgroups[attr] == grp).to_numpy()
            k, n = int((pred[m] == lbl_test[m]).sum()), int(m.sum())
            lo, hi = wilson_ci(k, n)
            rows.append({'Model': model_name, 'Attribute': attr, 'Subgroup': grp, 'n': n,
                         'Accuracy': k / n, 'CI low': lo, 'CI high': hi,
                         'Macro recall': recall_score(lbl_test[m], pred[m], average='macro'),
                         'Macro F1': f1_score(lbl_test[m], pred[m], average='macro')})
subgroup_results = pd.DataFrame(rows)
subgroup_results.to_csv('artifacts/subgroup_results.csv', index=False)
display(subgroup_results.round(4))

# Disparity summary + chi-square test of independence (is accuracy independent of subgroup?)
summary = []
for (model_name, attr), g in subgroup_results.groupby(['Model', 'Attribute'], sort=False):
    pred = test_predictions[model_name]
    table = pd.crosstab(subgroups[attr], pred == lbl_test)
    summary.append({'Model': model_name, 'Attribute': attr,
                    'Worst subgroup': g.loc[g['Accuracy'].idxmin(), 'Subgroup'],
                    'Best subgroup': g.loc[g['Accuracy'].idxmax(), 'Subgroup'],
                    'Accuracy gap (pts)': (g['Accuracy'].max() - g['Accuracy'].min()) * 100,
                    'Chi-square p-value': chi2_contingency(table)[1]})
disparity = pd.DataFrame(summary)
display(disparity.round(4))

E4. Controlled lighting experiment¶

Natural subgroups differ in more than brightness (e.g. dark images contain more night scenes, certain classes and less detail). To isolate the effect of lighting alone, the same 2,000 test images are artificially darkened or brightened by multiplying pixel values by a factor (clipped to the valid range) and re-evaluated. This simulates deployment conditions that differ from the training data (a form of distribution shift).

In [ ]:
# ====================================================
# E4. ACCURACY UNDER SIMULATED LIGHTING CHANGES
# ====================================================
factors = [0.25, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 1.0, 1.25, 1.5, 2.0]
light_idx = np.random.default_rng(0).choice(len(img_test), 2000, replace=False)
base_imgs, base_lbls = img_test[light_idx].astype(np.float32), lbl_test[light_idx]

lighting_rows = []
for f in factors:
    adjusted = np.clip(base_imgs * f, 0, 255).astype(np.uint8)
    for model_name, predict in predictors.items():
        lighting_rows.append({'Model': model_name, 'Brightness factor': f,
                              'Accuracy': (predict(adjusted) == base_lbls).mean()})
lighting_df = pd.DataFrame(lighting_rows)
lighting_df.to_csv('artifacts/lighting_experiment.csv', index=False)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(12, 9), gridspec_kw={'height_ratios': [2.2, 1]})

E5. Bias findings: SVM vs CNN¶

Natural subgroups¶

Attribute SVM: worst → best (gap) p-value CNN: worst → best (gap) p-value
Lighting Dark 62.4% → Bright 66.1% (3.8 pts) 0.005 Dark 86.7% → Bright 89.1% (2.4 pts) 0.011
Contrast Medium 62.9% → High 66.6% (3.7 pts) 0.004 Low 87.3% → Medium 88.0% (0.7 pts) 0.67 (not significant)
Colourfulness Medium 62.4% → Muted 66.7% (4.2 pts) 0.001 Medium 87.1% → Vivid 88.2% (1.1 pts) 0.40 (not significant)
  • Both models perform worse on dark images, and the gap is statistically significant for both. The CNN's gap is smaller in absolute terms, and its accuracy on dark images (86.7%) is still far higher than the SVM's best subgroup (66.7%).
  • The CNN is fair across contrast and colourfulness: the differences are small and not statistically significant. The SVM shows significant gaps on all three attributes.

The subgroups are confounded with class. Bright images contain far more airplanes (18%) and ships (13%), photographed against sky and sea, while dark images contain more frogs, cats and automobiles. For the SVM the class-balanced macro recall gap shrinks from 3.8 to 2.5 points, and for some classes the effect reverses (deer: 66% dark vs 54% bright). For the CNN the per-class heatmap shows the largest lighting effect for airplanes (84% dark vs 95% bright), while frogs are recognised slightly better in the dark (97% vs 92%). Part of any raw subgroup gap therefore reflects what is photographed under each condition, so subgroup gaps must be checked for confounders before concluding that a model is biased.

Controlled lighting experiment (same 2,000 images, only brightness changed)¶

Brightness factor 0.25 0.4 0.6 1.0 (original) 1.5 2.0
SVM 60.7% 61.7% 63.3% 63.4% 58.0% 44.2%
CNN 62.5% 82.3% 87.5% 88.5% 84.0% 70.9%
  • The CNN is highly sensitive to strong darkening: at 25% brightness it loses 26 points (88.5% → 62.5%) and falls to the SVM's level. The SVM loses only 3 points, because HOG normalises each block's gradients, which cancels out a uniform change in brightness. The CNN was trained on raw pixel intensities from mostly well-lit web photos and never saw very dark images, so it has not learned brightness invariance.
  • Both models suffer under over-exposure (2× brightness): the SVM drops 19 points and the CNN 18 points, because clipped white pixels erase edges and textures.
  • Within the normal range (60-150% brightness) the CNN stays above 82% and is better than the SVM at every level.

Real-world implications¶

This is a trade-off hidden by the headline accuracy: the more accurate model (CNN) is also the more fragile one under one specific condition, very low light. In the roadside wildlife scenario (Part F) this matters because many animals cross roads at dusk and at night, exactly when images are darkest. Errors would be concentrated on particular times of day and locations rather than spread randomly.

Mitigations: add brightness, contrast and gamma augmentation during training (the current augmentation changes geometry only); normalise exposure per image before inference; collect night-time and infrared training data; use cameras with good low-light performance; and monitor accuracy per lighting condition after deployment.

Part F: Ethical Considerations¶

To keep the discussion concrete, we consider a realistic deployment of a CIFAR-10-style classifier: a roadside camera that recognises animals (deer, horses, dogs, cats, birds, frogs) versus vehicles, to trigger wildlife-crossing warnings for drivers and to count animal crossings for conservation.

1. Data privacy: provenance, consent and personal data¶

  • Provenance: CIFAR-10 is a hand-labelled subset of the 80 Million Tiny Images collection (Torralba, Fergus & Freeman, 2008), which was gathered automatically from web image searches. Neither the photographers nor any people pictured gave consent, and image licences were not checked.
  • In 2020 MIT withdrew 80 Million Tiny Images after an audit (Prabhu & Birhane, 2020) found offensive labels and non-consensual images. CIFAR-10 uses only ten neutral, manually verified object classes and remains in use, but it inherits the same lack of consent.
  • Personally identifiable information: no class contains people and no labels describe individuals, but people, faces or number plates can appear incidentally (especially in automobile and truck images). At 32×32 pixels identification is practically impossible; a real roadside camera at full resolution, however, would capture faces and number plates, which are personal data under GDPR.
  • Mitigations for deployment: classify on the device and discard frames immediately, never store raw images by default, blur faces and plates if images must be kept for retraining, set strict retention limits, and complete a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA).

2. Algorithmic fairness: consequences of false positives and false negatives¶

Error Example Real-world consequence Severity
False negative (animal missed) a deer classified as a vehicle No warning → collision risk to the driver and the animal High: safety-critical
False positive (false alarm) a truck classified as a horse Unnecessary warning → alert fatigue: drivers learn to ignore the sign Medium
Confusion between animals cat ↔ dog Little effect on warnings, but distorts conservation counts Low-medium
  • The classical SVM recognises only 63% of deer (deer recall 0.63) and about 44% of cats; at that error rate the warning system would miss more than one in three deer. The CNN recognises 85% of deer and 70% of cats (Part A), far better but still not perfect for a safety-critical use.
  • Because a missed animal is much worse than a false alarm, the deployed model should be tuned for high recall on animal classes (e.g. a lower decision threshold for animals), accepting more false alarms.
  • Errors are not spread evenly. Part E shows that both models are significantly less accurate on dark images, and that under strong darkening the CNN loses 26 points (88% → 62%). Many animals cross roads at dusk and at night, exactly when images are darkest, so the system would fail most when it is needed most. Over-exposure (glare, strong sun) also costs both models 18-19 points. Errors would therefore cluster at specific times of day and locations, so some roads and habitats would receive a systematically worse service.

3. Bias and harm¶

  • Dataset bias: the images are web photographs: mostly daytime, well-framed, centred and taken by people who chose to upload them. A roadside camera sees night-time and infrared images, motion blur, rain, partial occlusion and animals at the edge of the frame. This distribution shift would lower real-world accuracy below the test-set figures.
  • Spurious correlations: LIME (Part D) showed the SVM classifying a bird as an airplane mainly because of the plain, sky-like background. A model relying on such shortcuts can fail badly in new environments.
  • Measured disparities: both models are significantly worse on dark images; the SVM also shows significant gaps for contrast and colourfulness, while the CNN does not (Part E). Part of these gaps is explained by differences in class composition.
  • Potential harms: physical (vehicle-animal collisions), environmental (wildlife mortality, wrong conservation decisions) and automation bias (operators over-trusting automated counts).
  • Mitigations: collect training data from the actual cameras, including night-time and infrared images; augment with brightness, contrast, blur and noise (the current augmentation is purely geometric); evaluate per subgroup before release; send low-confidence predictions to human review; document the model with a model card and the data with a datasheet.

4. Recommendation: which model to deploy?¶

The custom CNN is recommended. It is 23 accuracy points better than the SVM, better on every class including the safety-critical animal classes, generalises well (validation ≈ test), and its explanations show that it bases decisions on the object rather than background shortcuts (Part D). It also keeps improving as more data from real cameras is collected. The SVM's advantages (CPU-only training, simplicity and robustness to darkness) do not outweigh missing over a third of the deer.

The CNN should be deployed only with safeguards:

  1. Fix the low-light weakness before deployment: retrain with brightness/gamma augmentation and night-time images, and verify accuracy on dark images reaches an agreed minimum.
  2. Use high-recall thresholds for animal classes.
  3. Send low-confidence predictions (or diffuse Grad-CAM maps) to human review.
  4. Test per subgroup on local camera data before go-live, and monitor continuously afterwards (Part G).

Part G: Real-World Deployment Considerations¶

Proposed architecture¶

 Roadside camera ──► On-device model (TensorFlow Lite) ──► Warning sign / alert
        │                        │
        │ (low-confidence frames, anonymised)          prediction + confidence logs
        ▼                        ▼
 Cloud labelling queue ──► Vertex AI / SageMaker: model registry, retraining pipeline, monitoring dashboard

1. Packaging and serving

  • The trained CNN is exported as a Keras/SavedModel file. The preprocessing (resize to 32×32, scale to 0-1) is built into the serving function, so production inputs are processed exactly as during training (avoiding training-serving skew).
  • Edge option (recommended for this use case): convert to TensorFlow Lite with int8 quantisation (about 4× smaller, roughly 3-4 MB) and run it on the camera device. Benefits: low latency for real-time warnings, works without connectivity, and images never leave the device, which supports the privacy requirements in Part F.
  • Cloud option: deploy to a managed endpoint such as Google Vertex AI (a natural fit for a TensorFlow model trained on Colab), AWS SageMaker or Azure ML, exposed as a REST API (POST /predict with an image → {class, confidence}), or self-host with TF Serving or FastAPI in a Docker container.

2. Scalability

  • The model server is stateless, so it scales horizontally: the platform adds or removes replicas automatically with traffic.
  • Requests can be batched on a GPU for throughput. The model is small (3.4M parameters), so CPU inference is also affordable at moderate volume.
  • Edge deployment scales naturally: each new camera brings its own compute.

3. Monitoring

  • Data drift: track the brightness, contrast and colourfulness of incoming images (the same measures as in Part E) and alert when they move away from the training distribution, e.g. at night, after the season changes or when a camera is replaced. This is especially important because Part E showed the CNN's accuracy falling sharply on very dark images.
  • Prediction drift: track the distribution of predicted classes and average confidence; a sudden rise in low-confidence predictions signals a problem.
  • Performance and fairness: regularly have humans label a sample of images and track accuracy and recall per class and per subgroup (day/night, weather), not just overall.
  • Operational: latency, error rates and device health.

4. Retraining

  • Route low-confidence and disputed predictions (anonymised) to human labellers, building a growing dataset from the real cameras.
  • Retrain on a schedule or when drift is detected. A new model is promoted only if it beats the current one overall and on every monitored subgroup.
  • Roll out safely with a model registry (versioning), shadow or canary deployment (the new model runs in parallel before taking over) and the ability to roll back instantly.

5. Governance: keep a model card (intended use, limitations, subgroup performance), restrict access to logs and data, and review the system periodically for fairness and privacy compliance.

Conclusion¶

Question Answer
Which model performs better? The custom CNN: 87.7% accuracy and 0.875 macro F1 vs 64.4% / 0.643 for the HOG + RBF-SVM, and better on every class. Its largest gains are on visually similar animals (cat, bird, dog) where hand-crafted edge features fail.
Is the evaluation trustworthy? Yes. The SVM was validated with stratified 5-fold CV (63.0% ± 0.5), which closely predicted its test accuracy (64.4%). The CNN's best validation accuracy (88.1%) matched its test accuracy (87.7%). Validation also exposed the SVM's severe overfitting (99.7% training accuracy).
Why does the CNN win? It learns its features, while the SVM depends on hand-engineered HOG features that capture only edge shape (Part D: removing them reduces the SVM to chance; colour adds almost nothing).
What do the models look at? The CNN focuses on the object (Grad-CAM evidence concentrated in the centre; more diffuse when it is wrong). The SVM is more easily misled by backgrounds (e.g. a bird on a sky-like background → airplane).
Are the models biased? Both are significantly less accurate on dark images. The CNN is fair across contrast and colourfulness, the SVM is not. A controlled experiment revealed a hidden trade-off: the CNN loses 26 points on very dark images while the SVM barely changes, and both degrade under over-exposure.
What are the costs of deep learning? GPU training (~15 min vs ~2.5 min on a CPU), less inherent transparency, and fragility to conditions absent from the training data.
Which model should be deployed? The CNN, with safeguards: brightness augmentation and night-time data before release, high-recall thresholds for safety-critical classes, human review of uncertain predictions, privacy-preserving on-device inference (TensorFlow Lite), and continuous per-subgroup monitoring with a controlled retraining pipeline.

Key lesson: headline accuracy is not enough. Cross-validation, explainability and subgroup analysis each revealed something that the overall accuracy hid (overfitting, background shortcuts and lighting fragility). These are exactly the issues that determine whether a model is safe and fair to deploy in the real world.
